# Entropic Regularization and Sinkhorn {.title-slide}

<div class="subtitle">Fast differentiable optimal transport through entropy, scaling, and dual potentials.</div>

<div class="author-line">Gabriel Peyré</div>

<div class="affiliation-line">CNRS and École normale supérieure, PSL Université</div>

<div class="logo-line" style="margin-top:1.1rem;">Optimal Transport for Machine Learners</div>

## Why regularize OT?

<div class="two-col-wide">
<div>

Kantorovich OT is geometrically meaningful but often expensive and non-smooth as a function of the data.

Entropic regularization trades exact sparsity for:

- fast matrix scaling iterations,
- differentiable losses,
- stable dual potentials,
- better statistical behavior at fixed regularization.

</div>

</div>

## Discrete entropic OT

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Entropic regularization.</span>
For histograms $a\in\Sigma_n$, $b\in\Sigma_m$, cost matrix $C$, and $\varepsilon>0$,
$$
\mathcal L_{C,\varepsilon}(a,b)
=
\min_{P\in U(a,b)}
\langle C,P\rangle
+
\varepsilon\sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\big(\log P_{i,j}-1\big),
$$
where $U(a,b)=\{P\geq 0:P\mathbb 1_m=a,\ P^\top\mathbb 1_n=b\}$.
:::

The entropy term makes the objective strictly convex on the positive orthant.

## Relative entropy form

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">KL form.</span>
Using the product reference $a\otimes b$, the same minimization can be written, up to an additive constant independent of $P$, as
$$
\min_{P\in U(a,b)}
\langle C,P\rangle+
\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(P\mid a\otimes b),
$$
where
$$
\operatorname{KL}(P\mid Q)=\sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\log\frac{P_{i,j}}{Q_{i,j}}-P_{i,j}+Q_{i,j}.
$$
:::

This is the discrete static Schroedinger problem.

## Probabilistic interpretation

Let $(X,Y)$ have joint law $P$ and marginals $a,b$. Then
$$
\operatorname{KL}(P\mid a\otimes b)=I(X;Y),
$$
the mutual information between $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Interpretation.</span>
Entropic OT minimizes expected transport cost while penalizing dependence between the source and target labels.
:::

Small $\varepsilon$ allows near-deterministic transport. Large $\varepsilon$ pushes toward independence.

## Continuous formulation

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Continuous entropic OT.</span>
For probability measures $\alpha,\beta$,
$$
\mathcal L_{c,\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta)
=
\inf_{\pi\in\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)}
\int c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)
+
\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\mid \alpha\otimes\beta).
$$
Here $\operatorname{KL}(\pi\mid q)=\int\log(d\pi/dq)\,d\pi$ if $\pi\ll q$, and $+\infty$ otherwise.
:::

Under the usual compactness and lower-semicontinuity assumptions, the value converges to the Kantorovich cost as $\varepsilon\to0$.

## Schrödinger path-space viewpoint

<div class="two-col-wide">
<div>

A dynamic version replaces straight-line transport by a controlled Brownian bridge problem. The static coupling is the endpoint law of a path measure.

In the historical “lazy gas” interpretation of Schrödinger's problem, one observes an unlikely final cloud and asks for the most likely Brownian path ensemble producing it.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Static endpoint reduction.</span>
For Brownian reference dynamics, optimizing over path laws with fixed endpoint marginals reduces to an entropic problem over the endpoint coupling.
:::

</div>

## Sinkhorn scaling form

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Scaling form.</span>
Let $K=e^{-C/\varepsilon}$ with positive entries. The entropic optimizer is unique and satisfies
$$
P=\operatorname{diag}(u)K\operatorname{diag}(v),
$$
where $u\in\mathbb R_+^n$ and $v\in\mathbb R_+^m$ enforce the two marginals.
Equivalently,
$$
u\odot(Kv)=a,
\qquad
v\odot(K^\top u)=b.
$$
:::

This reduces a constrained convex optimization problem to a matrix scaling problem.

## Sinkhorn algorithm

::: {.algorithm-box}
<span class="box-title">Sinkhorn scaling / IPFP / RAS.</span>
Input: histograms $a,b$, kernel $K=e^{-C/\varepsilon}$.  
Output: scaled coupling $P$ with marginals $a,b$.

1. Initialize $v^{(0)}=\mathbb 1_m$.
2. For $\ell=0,1,2,\ldots$, update
$$
u^{(\ell+1)}=\frac{a}{K v^{(\ell)}},
\qquad
v^{(\ell+1)}=\frac{b}{K^\top u^{(\ell+1)}}.
$$
3. Return $P^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{diag}(u^{(\ell)})K\operatorname{diag}(v^{(\ell)})$.
:::

All divisions are entrywise.

The same matrix-scaling iteration appears under several names: Sinkhorn scaling, IPFP in statistics, and RAS in economics and input-output analysis.

## Matrix scaling has a long history

<div class="two-col-wide">
<div>

Sinkhorn is one member of a broader matrix-scaling family.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Sinkhorn, IPFP, RAS.</span>
Given a positive matrix $K$, the goal is to find diagonal scalings $u,v>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{diag}(u)K\operatorname{diag}(v)\mathbb 1=a,
\qquad
\operatorname{diag}(v)K^\top\operatorname{diag}(u)\mathbb 1=b.
$$
The same alternating normalization appears in statistics, economics, input-output tables, and entropy-regularized OT.
:::

The OT contribution is to choose the matrix as the Gibbs kernel $K=e^{-C/\varepsilon}$.

</div>

## Computational structure

For dense kernels, one Sinkhorn iteration costs $O(nm)$.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">When Sinkhorn is fast.</span>
Sinkhorn is fastest when $K$ has exploitable structure: convolution, separability, low rank, multiscale structure, or GPU-friendly matrix operations.
:::

This explains its role in machine learning: it is differentiable and easy to batch.

## Perron-Frobenius viewpoint

Hilbert-metric convergence comes from positive operators, not only from convex analysis.

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Positive operator intuition.</span>
A positive linear map contracts the projective geometry of the cone. Sinkhorn alternates two such positive maps, and the resulting contraction explains a linear convergence mechanism when the kernel is strictly positive and well conditioned.
:::

This is the conceptual bridge between classical Perron-Frobenius theory, Rothblum-type matrix-scaling convergence analyses, and the Hilbert-metric proof later in this deck.

## Other convex regularizers

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">General regularized OT.</span>
Entropy can be replaced by a convex divergence:
$$
\min_{P\in U(a,b)} \langle C,P\rangle+
\varepsilon D_\varphi(P\mid a\otimes b).
$$
For $Q=a\otimes b$, this means
$$
D_\varphi(P\mid Q)=\sum_{i,j}Q_{i,j}\,
\varphi\!\left(\frac{P_{i,j}}{Q_{i,j}}\right).
$$
:::

Different choices of $\varphi$ change both the smoothness and sparsity of the optimal coupling.

## Bregman projection view

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Iterative KL projections.</span>
Sinkhorn is alternating Bregman projection for the KL divergence onto the affine marginal constraint sets
$$
\mathcal C_a=\{P:P\mathbb 1_m=a\},
\qquad
\mathcal C_b=\{P:P^\top\mathbb 1_n=b\}.
$$
:::

The initial matrix is the Gibbs kernel $K=e^{-C/\varepsilon}$, and each projection is a multiplicative rescaling.

## Dual problem

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Entropic dual.</span>
The discrete entropic problem has dual
$$
\max_{f,g}
\langle f,a\rangle+\langle g,b\rangle
-
\varepsilon\sum_{i,j}a_i b_j
\left(e^{(f_i+g_j-C_{i,j})/\varepsilon}-1\right).
$$
At optimality,
$$
P_{i,j}=a_i b_j e^{(f_i+g_j-C_{i,j})/\varepsilon}.
$$
:::

With the convention $P=\operatorname{diag}(u)K\operatorname{diag}(v)$, one has
$u_i=a_i e^{f_i/\varepsilon}$ and $v_j=b_j e^{g_j/\varepsilon}$.

## Soft c-transforms

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Soft c-transform.</span>
For a function $f$ on the source support,
$$
f^{c,\varepsilon}(y_j)
=-\varepsilon\log\sum_i a_i
\exp\left(\frac{f_i-C_{i,j}}{\varepsilon}\right).
$$
:::

Dual block maximization alternates soft transforms:
$$
g\leftarrow f^{c,\varepsilon},
\qquad
f\leftarrow g^{\bar c,\varepsilon}.
$$

## Live panel: soft c-transforms

<div class="live-panel">
<iframe src="../../myst/live/sinkhorn-soft-c.html" title="Interactive soft c-transforms"></iframe>
</div>

Soft transforms replace hard envelopes by log-sum-exp envelopes.

## Stabilized log-domain Sinkhorn

For small $\varepsilon$, $K=e^{-C/\varepsilon}$ can underflow. Stabilized implementations store log-scalings, equivalently dual potentials.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Stabilized log-domain updates.</span>
Instead of scaling vectors $u,v$, store potentials
$$
f_i=\varepsilon\log(u_i/a_i),
\qquad
g_j=\varepsilon\log(v_j/b_j).
$$
The updates are soft $c$-transforms computed with log-sum-exp operations.
:::

This keeps the Sinkhorn iteration stable when $\varepsilon$ is small and the Gibbs kernel has entries below machine precision.

## Log-domain update steps

::: {.algorithm-box .small .compact-eq}
<span class="box-title">Stabilized Sinkhorn iteration.</span>
Input: histograms $a,b$, cost matrix $C$, regularization $\varepsilon>0$.  
Output: stabilized dual potentials $f,g$.

1. Initialize $f=0$.
2. Repeat until convergence:
$$
\begin{aligned}
g_j \leftarrow -\varepsilon\log\sum_i a_i
  \exp\!\left(\frac{f_i-C_{i,j}}{\varepsilon}\right),\\
f_i \leftarrow -\varepsilon\log\sum_j b_j
\exp\!\left(\frac{g_j-C_{i,j}}{\varepsilon}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
3. Recover $P_{i,j}=a_i b_j \exp((f_i+g_j-C_{i,j})/\varepsilon)$.
:::

This is numerically stable because it uses log-sum-exp operations.

## Hilbert projective metric

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Hilbert metric.</span>
For positive vectors $u,v$,
$$
d_H(u,v)=\log\max_i\frac{u_i}{v_i}
-
\log\min_i\frac{u_i}{v_i}.
$$
:::

It ignores global scaling. This is exactly what is needed because Sinkhorn scalings are unique only up to reciprocal multiplication.

## Linear contraction mechanism

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Positive maps contract projectively.</span>
Positive linear maps are nonexpansive in Hilbert metric, and strictly positive matrices contract under quantitative irreducibility assumptions.
:::

Applied to $K$ and $K^\top$, this yields linear convergence of Sinkhorn in a projective metric.

<div class="figure-row">
<img src="assets/linear-rate-errors.png" style="width:56%;max-height:205px" alt="Sinkhorn linear rate">
</div>

## Monotone and variation viewpoints

The log-domain map
$$
f\mapsto (f^{c,\varepsilon})^{\bar c,\varepsilon}
$$
is order-preserving and commutes with additive constants.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Topical-map intuition.</span>
Order preservation plus translation invariance implies nonexpansiveness for the variation seminorm
$$
\|f\|_{\mathrm{var}}=\max_i f_i-\min_i f_i.
$$
:::

This gives a robust way to read Sinkhorn as a monotone fixed-point iteration.

## Unbalanced entropic OT

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">KL-unbalanced formulation.</span>
Instead of enforcing exact marginals, penalize deviations:
$$
\min_{P\geq 0}
\langle C,P\rangle+
\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(P\mid a\otimes b)
+\tau\operatorname{KL}(P\mathbb 1\mid a)
+\tau\operatorname{KL}(P^\top\mathbb 1\mid b).
$$
:::

This allows mass creation and destruction when matching every unit of mass is unnatural.
The associated dynamic viewpoint is geodesic unbalanced OT: particles can move while their mass is also allowed to grow or decay.

## Live panel: unbalanced entropic transport

<div class="live-panel">
<iframe src="../../myst/live/generalized-unbalanced.html" title="Interactive unbalanced entropic transport"></iframe>
</div>

Relaxing marginal constraints changes transport into a combined displacement and mass-variation problem.

## Generalized Sinkhorn for unbalanced OT

For the KL marginal penalty, the updates become damped:
$$
u\leftarrow \left(\frac{a}{K v}\right)^{\tau/(\tau+\varepsilon)},
\qquad
v\leftarrow \left(\frac{b}{K^\top u}\right)^{\tau/(\tau+\varepsilon)}.
$$

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Balanced limit.</span>
As $\tau\to +\infty$, the exponent tends to one and one recovers ordinary Sinkhorn scaling.
:::

## Entropic barycenters

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Entropic Wasserstein barycenter.</span>
Given input measures $(\beta_s)_s$ and weights $(\lambda_s)_s$, compute
$$
\min_\alpha \sum_s \lambda_s\mathcal L_{c,\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta_s).
$$
:::

Sinkhorn-like updates alternate between transport couplings and the barycenter weights.

## Kernel norms and MMD

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">MMD.</span>
For a reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal H$,
$$
\operatorname{MMD}_k(\alpha,\beta)
=
\sup_{\|f\|_\mathcal H\leq 1}
\int f\,d(\alpha-\beta).
$$
:::

MMD is not an OT distance, but it is another differentiable discrepancy with favorable sample complexity.

<div class="figure-row">
<img src="assets/mmd-witness.png" style="width:46%;max-height:170px" alt="MMD witness">
</div>

## Sinkhorn divergence

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Debiased Sinkhorn loss.</span>
The Sinkhorn divergence is
$$
S_\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)
=
\mathcal L_{c,\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta)
-\frac12\mathcal L_{c,\varepsilon}(\alpha,\alpha)
-\frac12\mathcal L_{c,\varepsilon}(\beta,\beta).
$$
:::

The correction removes the entropic self-bias: $S_\varepsilon(\alpha,\alpha)=0$, while preserving differentiability.

## Positivity and limits

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Sinkhorn divergence behavior.</span>
For many standard costs, $S_\varepsilon$ is nonnegative and separates probability measures. Moreover,
$$
S_\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)\to W_c(\alpha,\beta)
\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to 0,
$$
while large $\varepsilon$ connects to kernel norms and MMD-type limits.
:::

This gives a continuum between OT geometry and kernel discrepancies.

## Curse of dimensionality for exact OT

For empirical measures $\hat\alpha_n$, exact OT suffers from dimension-dependent rates:
$$
\mathbb E\, W_p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)
\asymp n^{-1/d}
$$
in the high-dimensional absolutely continuous regime, up to known endpoint variations.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Message.</span>
Exact OT is geometrically rich but statistically expensive in high dimension.
:::

## Fixed $\varepsilon$ changes the statistics

At fixed $\varepsilon>0$, entropic OT and Sinkhorn divergences are smoother functionals of the empirical measure.

::: {.theorem-box}
<span class="box-title">Parametric behavior at fixed $\varepsilon$.</span>
Under regularity assumptions, empirical Sinkhorn divergences admit $n^{-1/2}$-type fluctuations, with constants depending on $\varepsilon$.
:::

The price is bias: fixed $\varepsilon$ does not equal exact OT.

<div class="two-col">
<div>

Small $\varepsilon$ reduces bias but makes computation and statistics harder. Large $\varepsilon$ smooths the problem but changes the geometry.

The useful regime balances approximation bias against statistical variance.

## Entropy estimates exact OT through three errors

For empirical data, the approximation to exact OT contains:

1. sampling error,
2. regularization bias,
3. numerical optimization error.

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Practical rule.</span>
Choose $\varepsilon$ large enough for stable estimation and fast Sinkhorn iterations, but small enough to retain the desired OT geometry.
:::

## Smoothness and high dimension

<div class="two-col-wide">
<div>

If the inputs have smooth densities, smoothing or regularization can exploit this smoothness. In high dimension, generic smoothing is itself costly.

This is one reason entropic OT is attractive in practice: it provides a differentiable approximation with scalable linear-algebra structure.

</div>

## Generative model fitting

<div class="two-col-wide">
<div>

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="box-title">Sinkhorn training loss.</span>
For a generator $g_\theta$ and latent law $\zeta$, train with
$$
\min_\theta
S_\varepsilon\big((g_\theta)_\#\zeta,\beta\big).
$$
:::

The differentiability of the entropic problem makes this compatible with automatic differentiation.
Historically, the same training loop was used in Wasserstein, Sinkhorn, and MMD generative models, including progressive growing GAN experiments.

</div>
<div class="panel tight">
<img src="assets/ref-generative-images.png" alt="Image-generation examples with OT-type losses">
</div>
</div>

## Discriminator versus generator viewpoint

Kantorovich dual potentials play the role of smooth discriminators:
$$
\nabla_\theta S_\varepsilon((g_\theta)_\#\zeta,\beta)
$$
can be computed by differentiating through the generator and using the optimal dual potentials or coupling.

<div class="figure-row">
<img src="assets/gen-ot-rays.png" style="width:31%" alt="Generative optimal transport rays">
<img src="assets/gen-sinkhorn-field.png" style="width:31%" alt="Generative Sinkhorn vector field">
<img src="assets/gen-mmd-field.png" style="width:31%" alt="Generative MMD vector field">
</div>

## Automatic differentiation

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Envelope principle.</span>
Once the optimal dual variables are computed, the derivative of the regularized transport value with respect to the cost is the optimal coupling:
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal L_{C,\varepsilon}}{\partial C_{i,j}}=P_{i,j}^\star.
$$
With respect to weights, the derivatives are the optimal dual potentials, up to the usual additive normalization.
:::

This is the basic reason Sinkhorn losses integrate well into differentiable learning pipelines.

## Training architecture

<div class="two-col">
<div>

A typical mini-batch pipeline is:

1. sample latent variables and data,
2. build the cost matrix,
3. run Sinkhorn iterations,
4. backpropagate the Sinkhorn loss through the generator.

</div>
<div class="panel">
<img src="assets/gen-w2-svgd.png" alt="Generative particles">
</div>
</div>

## Open problems and design tensions

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Main tension.</span>
Entropic OT is an approximation, a numerical method, a statistical smoother, and a differentiable loss. The best $\varepsilon$ depends on the role.
:::

Open directions include scalable approximations in high dimension, adaptive regularization, metric learning for costs, and robust generative training.

## Summary

<div class="three-col">
<div class="panel center"><strong>Entropy</strong><br><span class="muted">smooths OT plans</span></div>
<div class="panel center"><strong>Sinkhorn</strong><br><span class="muted">solves by scaling</span></div>
<div class="panel center"><strong>Debiasing</strong><br><span class="muted">turns costs into losses</span></div>
</div>

::: {.result-box}
<span class="box-title">Takeaway.</span>
Entropic regularization transforms optimal transport into a scalable differentiable primitive for optimization, statistics, and learning.
:::
